title: p99/p95 latency deep dive with Sable Robotics
summary: Redwood SE (Priya) walked Sable's infra team through tail-latency sources (p95/p99) focusing on KV cache cold/warm effects, batching tradeoffs for throughput vs tail, quantization implications, and network hops for VPC/on-prem. Agreed to run an end-to-end benchmark (streaming and non-streaming) with representative request mix; SE to produce an instrumentation checklist and sample tracing correlation. Next steps: benchmark run, share deck + spreadsheet, schedule 1-week follow-up.
topics: observability and tracing for tail analysis

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-05-07 15:00 PDT | Duration: 64 mins | Attendees: Jordan Mills, Priya Shah, Evan Park, Maya Chen, Luis Ortega

[00:00] Jordan Mills: Hey everyone thanks for joining, um we're gonna jump into the p95/p99 tail latency deep dive, Priya's gonna lead the technical pieces. Evan, Maya, Luis — thanks for making time.
[00:12] Evan Park: Thanks Jordan, yeah excited, p99s are biting us in prod, user experience spikes on longer orchestration tasks.
[00:20] Priya Shah: Cool, quick agenda: we'll cover observed p95/p99 behavior, KV cache cold/warm, batching windows and continuous batching, streaming vs non-streaming, quantization impacts, and network hop effects for your VPC setup. We'll finish with instrumentation checklist and next steps.
[00:35] Maya Chen: Heads up — our traffic is mix of short assistant queries and long generation prompts, about 30% > 512 tokens. We're seeing p99s around 800-1,200ms for the long ones, p95 around 220-300ms baseline.
[00:50] Priya Shah: Thanks, that's helpful. First principle: p95 mostly reflects typical path with some queuing; p99 is sensitive to rare events — cold KV cache, long GC or kernel retries, network retransmits, or pathological batching interactions.
[01:05] Luis Ortega: Quick question — when you say KV cache cold vs warm, are we talking per-request prefix hit rate or warm per-worker memory?
[01:12] Priya Shah: Both. Two levels: prefix/KV cache on the serving runtime that avoids recomputing attention states on repeated prefixes, and GPU-level warm caches like cuBLAS heuristics and CUDA page residency. If the prefix is cold you pay for recompute and larger KV writes which increases tail.
[01:30] Evan Park: Our big spikes match times when we have lots of unique user prompts, so KV cold seems plausible.
[01:36] Priya Shah: Also batching: continuous batching increases throughput but can increase p99 when a large request blocks a batch window or the batch formation waits for a large token length. For shorter prompt distributions you can tune max_batch_delay_ms and max_batch_tokens.
[01:52] Jordan Mills: And streaming helps with perceived latency for first token but can complicate tail metrics because streaming keeps connection open longer — so p99 token-to-token jitter matters.
[02:06] Maya Chen: We use streaming in UI. Our users complain mainly on completion time though.
[02:11] Priya Shah: Right — streaming reduces time-to-first-byte; it doesn't avoid full generation cost. For p95 you may see benefits, but p99 might still be dominated by long-run compute or network issues.
[02:25] Evan Park: Network hops — our setup is dev VPC -> NLB -> Redwood private connector -> Redwood runtime in partner region. How much hop-count contributes?
[02:36] Priya Shah: Each hop adds latency and variance. Key things: NLB connection reuse, TCP/TLS handshake rates, and proxy timeouts. For p99, transient packet loss or low-level retransmits can add hundreds of ms. Also cold TLS session resumption can add RTTs.
[02:55] Luis Ortega: We use mTLS inside, but the connector still crosses AZs sometimes. Do you have guidance on affinity or placement to reduce cross-AZ hops?
[03:03] Priya Shah: Affinity to local AZ or colocating runtime in same region reduces RTT. For Dedicated/Private, pinning the pool and avoiding cross-AZ routing is recommended. We can also adjust keepalive and connection pooling.
[03:16] Jordan Mills: Priya, can you talk about quantization effects on tail variance?
[03:20] Priya Shah: Sure. Lower-bit quant (4-bit or int8) reduces per-token compute but can introduce kernel divergence for certain layers and token lengths — some kernels fall back to slower paths when sparsity or fused ops misalign. That fallback can show as rare spikes in p99. Also quantized models may have different memory traffic patterns that interact with NVLink or PCIe causing jitter.
[03:44] Maya Chen: We were considering 4-bit to save costs. The tradeoffs on tail worry us.
[03:49] Priya Shah: It's often fine for p95, but we recommend staged runs: compare warm-cache vs cold-cache with representative workloads and track kernel fallback rates in profiler. Our Optimize team can produce config recommendations (per-layer quantization, fallback thresholds).
[04:05] Evan Park: About batching: what's your recommended max_batch_delay for interactive assistant style traffic?
[04:12] Priya Shah: If you want low latency, keep max_batch_delay <= 5ms and smaller max_batch_tokens. If throughput matters more and tail is acceptable, you can push delay higher. But note p99 often spikes when a large token-length request enters a small batch window — consider dynamic batching by length.
[04:30] Luis Ortega: Does Redwood runtime support per-route batching profiles? We have short small prompts and occasional long sequences.
[04:36] Priya Shah: Yes, per-route configs are supported. You can set different policies for assistant-short and long-gen routes and use routing policy to send long jobs to a larger pool or lower-cost pool with different SLOs.
[04:47] Jordan Mills: Let's dig into instrumentation — Priya you mentioned a checklist?
[04:51] Priya Shah: Yep. Things to capture: request timestamps at client send, gateway arrival, runtime accept, queue wait, batch start, token generation latencies (first byte, per-token), KV cache hit/miss, kernel fallback flags, GPU utilization, PCIe transfer times, network hop RTTs with traceroute-like spans, and TLS handshake markers. Correlate with request IDs.
[05:15] Maya Chen: Can you share a sample span map?
[05:18] Priya Shah: I'll share a sample diagram and a small OpenTelemetry schema. We'll include how to tag spans for prefix-hit vs prefix-miss.
[05:27] Evan Park: For our first run, how long should we run benchmarks and what mixes?
[05:31] Priya Shah: At least 24h if possible to capture diurnal patterns and rare events. Do cold-cache runs (after service restart) and warm runs. Mix should mirror prod: e.g. 60% short (<64 tokens), 30% medium (64-512), 10% long (>512). Also include burst patterns and sudden ramp-ups.
[05:49] Luis Ortega: Anything to watch with VPC connectors? We had occasional conn resets overnight.
[05:54] Priya Shah: Keepalive and connection pools, enable connection reuse on NLB, and track TCP retransmits. We can add health-check hooks and longer idle timeouts for long streaming connections. Also, look at MTU and NIC offload settings if you see fragmentation.
[06:10] Maya Chen: Regarding fallback to smaller models for load shedding — thoughts?
[06:14] Priya Shah: Good strategy: route to smaller, faster model when latency SLO at risk. But be careful about quality regression. Redwood supports automatic fallback policies with percentage-based rollouts so you can A/B test.
[06:27] Evan Park: Any quick wins to reduce p99 we can do before we run full benchmark?
[06:30] Priya Shah: Warm KV cache (keep warm workers), reduce cross-AZ routing, tune batch delay small for interactive routes, and improve connection reuse on NLB. Also, enable prefix caching for common prompts.
[06:44] Jordan Mills: We'll want the deck and spreadsheet — Jordan to send?
[06:47] Jordan Mills: Yeah I'll drop both after the call. Priya will include the instrumentation checklist and OpenTelemetry schema.
[06:55] Maya Chen: Can you also include recommended quantization profiles for Llama-like models?
[06:59] Priya Shah: Yes, we'll include a starter profile: mixed 4-bit for attention + 8-bit for feedforward as an experimental baseline and notes on kernel fallback tuning.
[07:10] Evan Park: For the follow-up, can we include an SE-level run where you guys help interpret profiler output?
[07:15] Priya Shah: Absolutely — we can do a co-run and triage session.
[07:19] Jordan Mills: Great, recap of next steps: SE to run E2E benchmark (streaming + non-streaming), customer to provide traffic sample, SE to send instrumentation checklist and deck, schedule follow-up. Anything else?
[07:29] Luis Ortega: One small ask — include sample load tests that simulate jitter and packet loss.
[07:34] Priya Shah: We'll add a section in the spreadsheet for fault injection scenarios (3% packet drop, 100ms added RTT, etc).
[07:42] Evan Park: Thanks all.
[07:44] Jordan Mills: Thanks everyone, we'll send over items and get the follow-up scheduled.

Notes / Artifacts referenced: Deck: https://redwood.ai/decks/p99-deep-dive.pdf (placeholder link), Benchmark spreadsheet: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/sable-traffic-sample.xlsx, OpenTelemetry schema example (to be attached).

End of transcript.
